case_title: Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. v. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (first accused is the victim's wife); second accused is the wife's father, a relative by marriage of the victim
statutory_provisions: IPC s.420, s.468, s.471, s.120-B, s.201, each read with s.34; Passports Act 1967 s.12(b)
evidence_type: Documentary (passport application, sponsorship letter, State FSL report, private Truth Lab report)
mitigating_circumstances: The Court noted the passport motivation was not rooted in deceit, and the grant conferred no benefit on the first accused and caused no loss to the victim
trial_court_outcome: Discharge refused on 15.03.2018; charges to proceed under s.420 r/w s.34 IPC and other charges
neutral_facts: The victim and the first accused married in 2007, and a male child was born in 2008. Around January 2009, a passport application for the minor child was submitted to the Regional Passport Office, Bengaluru, and a passport was issued shortly afterwards. The victim alleges that his signatures on that passport application were forged and that the application was submitted while he was outside the country. The accused side contends that the victim had consented to the passport and later sent a sponsorship letter citing the child's passport number. The victim lodged a complaint on 13 May 2010, registered as an FIR under sections 420, 468 and 471 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The first accused had earlier complained of cruelty by the victim and his family. During the investigation, the charges under sections 468 and 471 were initially dropped. The State Forensic Laboratory expressed no opinion on the questioned photocopied signatures, citing bad line quality of strokes. A private laboratory report obtained by the victim, dated 15 July 2013, opined that the signatures did not closely resemble the victim's specimen signatures. A passport officer was implicated for allegedly withholding the original passport application. A supplementary chargesheet was later filed.
offence_severity: Section 420 IPC: imprisonment up to seven years and fine (no minimum stated)
motive: The Court accepted that the passport was meant for the child to join the family in London, not for deceit
key_evidence_accepted: State FSL report (inconclusive on forgery) relied on; private Truth Lab report found unreliable without corroboration; no new evidence from further investigation
trial_duration: offence: 13.07.2008 to 17.11.2009 (period argued by respondent's counsel); trial judgment: 15.03.2018 (trial magistrate order refusing discharge); High Court: 18.02.2021; Supreme Court: 22.01.2024
legal_representation: Appellants: Ranbir Singh Yadav, Mohammed Sharookh, Prateek Yadav, Anzu K. Varkey, Mahesh Sharma, Chembugari Abheeshna (Advocates). Respondents: Narendra Hodda, Sr. Adv., with Sanchit Garga, R. D. Singh, Mithu Jain, Kunal Rana, Pranshu Kaushal (Advocates); State counsel not separately named
investigation_status: FIR registered; chargesheet filed (468/471 dropped); further investigation ordered; supplementary chargesheet filed 25.07.2017
procedural_irregularity: Supplementary chargesheet filed without new evidence under s.173(8) CrPC; investigation mechanical; Trial Magistrate overlooked that the offences relate to matrimonial dispute rather than property offences
appeal_history: Trial court: discharge refused 15.03.2018. High Court: revision dismissed 18.02.2021. Supreme Court: appeal allowed; FIR and all proceedings quashed
prosecution_argument: Respondent's counsel argued the victim was abroad when the forged application was submitted; the Passport Officer withheld the original application; the Truth Lab report should not be discarded at discharge stage and its veracity should be tested at trial
defence_argument: Victim consented to the passport and sent the sponsorship letter citing its number; State FSL report was inconclusive and should prevail over paid private report; no prima facie case; complaint was a counterblast to the cruelty complaint; discharge sought under Krishna Chawla
legal_principle_applied: Cheating (s.420) requires deception, dishonest inducement to deliver property, and dishonest intention from inception, with damage or injury; forgery requires fabrication of a false document with dishonest intent; s.173(8) further investigation requires fresh evidence; continuing proceedings without these ingredients is abuse of process
precedent_relied_upon: Sushil Suri v. CBI (2011) 5 SCC 708 (forgery and dishonest intent); Vinay Tyagi v. Irshad Ali (2013) 5 SCC 762 (supplementary report); Krishna Chawla v. State of UP (2021) 5 SCC 435 (cited by appellants); Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248; K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2019) 1 SCC 1
judicial_mitigating_factors: Passport motivation not deceitful; no benefit to first accused and no loss to victim; second accused gained nothing; victim's conduct (counter-complaint, abandonment) weighed
other_sentence_order: Costs of Rs. 1,00,000 payable by the victim to the first accused within six weeks, failing which the Trial Magistrate to initiate coercive recovery
